Strait2005.species: Macaca fascicularis skull model; elastic-property data from M. mulatta skulls and human limb bones
Strait2005.measurement: In vivo strain data; measurement method not stated
Strait2005.materials: Analysis 1: isotropic properties from human limb bones; 2: one isotropic set from M. mulatta skulls; 3: region-specific isotropic sets; 4: region-specific orthotropic sets
Strait2005.agreement_metric: Strain comparison with in vivo data; metric and exact numbers not stated
Strait2005.result: Analysis 4, with region-specific orthotropic properties, deformed most realistically; exact quantitative agreement not stated
Strait2005.lessons: Imprecise elastic-property modeling can adversely affect results. Use properties from the relevant species and skeletal elements when possible.

Kupczik2007.loading: Non-physiological loads applied to the zygomatic arch; compared loading through a modeled superficial masseter with loading an array of arch nodes.
Kupczik2007.measurement: Ex vivo strain-gauge measurements; maximum principal strains.
Kupczik2007.materials: Elastic properties for zygomatic arch bone and zygomaticotemporal suture obtained by nanoindentation; specific values not stated.
Kupczik2007.agreement_metric: Quantitative metric and exact values not stated.
Kupczik2007.result: High congruence between experimental and simulated strains; no exact numbers stated. Including a suture matched experimental strains better than modeling a separated or fused arch.
Kupczik2007.lessons: Accurate material properties and suture representation strongly affect predicted strains. Masseter loading produced distinctly higher strains than node-array loading; account for craniofacial sutures in functional analyses.

Ross2011.species: Macaques; Homo and Gorilla are mentioned for comparison.
Ross2011.loading: Mastication; FEM models cranial deformation during feeding.
Ross2011.measurement: In vivo bone strain; instrument type not stated.
Ross2011.result: not stated; no quantitative model–experiment agreement reported.
Ross2011.lessons: The FEM proposes inferior bending and twisting of the zygomatic arches, deforming the orbital and infraorbital regions. Relatively high strain in the anterior zygoma root suggests its morphology may help resist feeding forces.

Szwedowski2011.loading: Simulated physiological-like loading through the masseter and temporalis muscles
Szwedowski2011.materials: Material property assignment not stated; baseline model used locally defined cortical bone thicknesses
Szwedowski2011.result: Baseline subject-specific model with locally defined cortical bone thicknesses had the strongest correlation with experimental data (r² = 0.73).
Szwedowski2011.lessons: Small changes in cortical thickness caused large changes in strain patterns. Thin craniofacial bone structures are crucial for accurately characterizing local load distribution.

BrightRayfield2011.loading: Experimental loading conditions were applied, but load type, magnitude, and direction are not stated.
BrightRayfield2011.measurement: Ex vivo bone strains measured with strain gauges; CT scans were used to build the FE model.
BrightRayfield2011.materials: Isotropic homogeneous model; also heterogeneous isotropic models with a constant-thickness, stiffer cortical outer layer and more compliant cancellous interior. Property values not stated.
BrightRayfield2011.agreement_metric: Compared principal strain magnitudes, ratios, orientations, and contour patterns; no exact agreement statistics stated.
BrightRayfield2011.result: Loading conditions and principal strain orientations were predicted well, but some locations had incorrect principal strain magnitudes and ratios. Initial model was approximately an order of magnitude too stiff.
BrightRayfield2011.lessons: Models were most sensitive to material properties; a compliant interior improved strain magnitudes without notably affecting orientations, ratios, or contours. Local heterogeneity and limited CT resolution may explain discrepancies. Use caution for absolute breaking stress or bite-force estimates; relative comparisons may be robust.

BrightGroning2011.materials: Suture modeled with 3D elements assigned more compliant properties than surrounding bone; no values stated.
BrightGroning2011.result: No quantitative model–experiment agreement values stated. Compliant solid sutures best reproduced the experiment; no-suture models were nearly indistinguishable except near the suture.
BrightGroning2011.lessons: A solid, flexible suture model is preferred. Open mesh breaks and spring elements failed to reproduce the experiment; suture detail may be unnecessary for whole-skull behavior in pigs.

Groning2012.measurement: Digital speckle pattern interferometry (DSPI) full-field strain measurements
Groning2012.materials: Homogeneous, isotropic mechanical properties; values not stated
Groning2012.agreement_metric: not stated; no quantitative metric or exact values given
Groning2012.result: The two models predicted measured strain directions and magnitudes surprisingly well, but agreement varied across and between measurement areas.
Groning2012.lessons: Full-field comparisons provide more comprehensive validation than point measurements and reveal spatial variation and discrepancies, likely due to model geometry inaccuracies and simplified material properties.

Groning2009.loading: Loaded human mandible; load type and magnitude not stated
Groning2009.measurement: Digital speckle pattern interferometry (DSPI), full-field strain measurement
Groning2009.materials: Voxel-based model; material property assignment not stated
Groning2009.result: Qualitatively, FE-predicted strains corresponded well with experimental data; no quantitative values stated
Groning2009.lessons: DSPI provided consistent, reliable measurements and is useful for future bone-mechanics validation. The voxel-based model predicted experimental results accurately.

ToroIbacache2016.measurement: Digital speckle interferometry measured strains in the infraorbital region and frontal process of the maxilla
ToroIbacache2016.materials: Compared cancellous bone represented as solid cortical bone; other material properties not stated
ToroIbacache2016.agreement_metric: Qualitative comparison of strain distributions, magnitudes, and directions; quantitative metric not stated
ToroIbacache2016.result: The most detailed model generally reproduced in-vitro patterns of relatively high and low principal strains and strain-vector magnitudes and directions; exact numbers not stated.
ToroIbacache2016.lessons: Treating cancellous bone as cortical substantially lowered strain magnitudes but preserved deformation mode. Omitting thin circum-nasal bone altered both mode and magnitude. Interpret and compare cranial FEA results cautiously.

Panagiotopoulou2017.loading: Muscle forces estimated at the time of maximum strain magnitude in the lower lateral gauge; chewing-side TMJ, premolars, and m1 constrained in X, Y, and Z; balancing-side TMJ constrained anterior-posterior and superior-inferior.
Panagiotopoulou2017.measurement: In vivo mandibular bone strain measurements at multiple strain locations; lower lateral strain gauge used to time muscle-force estimates.
Panagiotopoulou2017.materials: Trabecular bone modeled as isotropic and homogeneous, with Young’s modulus 10 GPa and Poisson’s ratio 0.3; tooth properties not stated.
Panagiotopoulou2017.agreement_metric: No quantitative agreement metric or values stated.
Panagiotopoulou2017.result: Relative strain magnitudes in the best-matching model were similar to in vivo measurements at all strain locations.
Panagiotopoulou2017.lessons: Model fit depended on trabecular material assumptions, joint and bite-point constraints, and muscle-force timing. Further analyses of strain patterns at different times during the chewing-cycle power stroke are needed.

Fitton2015.species: Macaca fascicularis; another comparison species is mentioned but not identified.
Fitton2015.measurement: none (computational strain maps and Procrustes size/shape analyses)
Fitton2015.materials: Tooth material properties were varied; specific assignments and values are not stated. Models also varied in segmentation detail, including a solid model.
Fitton2015.agreement_metric: not stated; no quantitative model-versus-experiment agreement metric reported.
Fitton2015.result: No exact quantitative agreement values reported. Models clustered by bite point rather than simplification approach.
Fitton2015.lessons: Simplifications had minimal impact on large-scale deformation, but localized strain magnitudes—especially in the alveolar region—varied. Simplify with care; fossil models may still yield reliable general deformation modes despite unknown internal architecture.

Porro2013.loading: In vivo feeding and biting at different bite locations
Porro2013.measurement: In vivo bone strain measurements at various sites on the lower jaw; specific instrument not stated
Porro2013.agreement_metric: Qualitative comparison of principal strain orientations, magnitudes, and mandibular deformation; no quantitative metric reported
Porro2013.result: FE model strain orientations and deformation closely matched in vivo results, but predicted absolute strain magnitudes were lower.
Porro2013.lessons: Working-side mandible underwent dorsoventral bending and long-axis twisting; balancing side primarily underwent dorsoventral bending and had higher strain magnitudes. No cause of model error or recommendation stated.

Provatidis2006.loading: Rapid maxillary expansion by jackscrew activation; modeled as one-step total activation or multiple steps accounting for stress relaxation.
Provatidis2006.measurement: Opening/displacement at four points (MI, UM, EM, CN) on both maxillae; measurement technique not stated.
Provatidis2006.result: Quantitative model–experiment agreement values not stated. Both show pyramidal maxillary opening.
Provatidis2006.lessons: Suture ossification influenced craniofacial displacement distribution more than stress relaxation; suture properties are important in the model.

Boryor2010.loading: Increasing transversal force applied to the alveolar process until rupture.
Boryor2010.measurement: Strain on the zygomatic process, maxilla displacement, and expanding forces were measured.
Boryor2010.lessons: The study recommends appropriate models. Adult tooth-anchored ultra-rapid expansion is unlikely to open the maxillary suture; complications or rupture may occur. Female specimens ruptured at lower forces; force–strain behavior was linear within each gender group.

Valeri2024.measurement: Load-displacement curves; secant stiffness and ultimate capacity
Valeri2024.lessons: Higher torque increased capacity with little effect on stiffness; torque strongly influenced push-in results, screw length influenced pull-out capacity, and diameter particularly affected shear stiffness.

Schileo2007.loading: Six different non-destructive in vitro loading scenarios; specific loads not stated.
Schileo2007.measurement: Strain gauges: 15 rosettes per femur, mostly in metaphyses; CT data used for model generation.
Schileo2007.materials: Three literature-derived density-elasticity power relationships assigned using CT data; specific values not stated.
Schileo2007.agreement_metric: R² and RMSE comparing FE-predicted strains with strain-gauge measurements
Schileo2007.result: One constitutive law achieved R²=0.91 and RMSE below 10% of the maximum measured value.
Schileo2007.lessons: The density-elasticity relationship strongly influenced prediction accuracy. A single relationship across the full bone-density range can provide accuracy suitable for many applications.

Schileo2008.measurement: CT density from CT images; apparent and ash densities measured experimentally; strain prediction assessed, measurement method not stated
Schileo2008.materials: Density relationships incorporated into subject-specific FE models; constant ash/apparent-density ratio assumed for the full density range
Schileo2008.lessons: CT-to-ash calibration correction avoids density-dependent bias. A constant ash/apparent-density ratio is supported; applying the relationships improved strain predictions and is recommended for subject-specific bone modelling.

Taddei2007.loading: Five different loading conditions; load types and magnitudes not stated.
Taddei2007.measurement: Experimental measurements at 13 strain-gauge locations; superficial stresses and strains.
Taddei2007.materials: Compared element Young’s modulus from average element density with the average of voxel-derived Young’s moduli; numerical property values not stated.
Taddei2007.agreement_metric: Stress and strain compared with experiments using regression coefficient, slope, average error, and peak error.
Taddei2007.result: Both strategies predicted stress accurately (regression coefficients >0.9; slopes not significantly different from 1). For strain, regression coefficient improved from 0.69 to 0.79; average error fell from 45.1% to 31.3%, and peak error from 228% to 134% of maximum measured strain.
Taddei2007.lessons: The strategies produced statistically different results. Averaging voxel-derived Young’s moduli improved strain prediction; internal stress fields also differed significantly. A software implementation of this strategy was made publicly available.

Keyak1993.loading: Load applied to the femoral head; magnitude not stated
Keyak1993.measurement: Strain gauges at 11 locations measured bone strain
Keyak1993.agreement_metric: Linear regression of predicted versus experimentally measured strains; P < 0.001
Keyak1993.result: Regression was significant; no quantitative agreement values stated
Keyak1993.lessons: The method was considered valid for predicting strain; surface-strain verification supported internal strain and stress predictions. Authors recommend the method as a research tool and for possible clinical applications.

Yosibash2007.loading: Quasi-static force up to 1500 N at four different angles
Yosibash2007.measurement: Vertical displacement and strains at various locations
Yosibash2007.materials: Inhomogeneous isotropic elastic properties assigned as distinct continuous spatial fields for cortical and trabecular regions; Young’s modulus fitted by least mean squares; values not stated
Yosibash2007.agreement_metric: Quantitative agreement metric and exact numbers not stated
Yosibash2007.result: Good agreement for displacement; fair agreement for strain at some locations
Yosibash2007.lessons: p-FEM bounded numerical error and quantified modeling assumptions; sensitivity was investigated, but error drivers were not stated. Study is a first step toward reliable QCT-based femur simulation for clinical decision making.

Trabelsi2011.loading: Simple stance-position load applied to the femoral head
Trabelsi2011.measurement: QCT scans; femoral surface strains and femoral-head displacements measured experimentally
Trabelsi2011.materials: Inhomogeneous micromechanics-based orthotropic properties or empirically determined isotropic properties
Trabelsi2011.agreement_metric: No quantitative agreement metric or values stated
Trabelsi2011.result: Both FE material models were in close qualitative agreement with experiments; orthotropic and isotropic predictions also matched well overall.
Trabelsi2011.lessons: Orthotropic properties produced more pronounced differences from isotropic predictions when comparing femoral-neck strains. Results support applying realistic inhomogeneous orthotropic properties in femur FEA.

Grassi2016.loading: Single loading condition; load type not stated.
Grassi2016.measurement: Digital image correlation (full-field surface strains); experimental fracture force and location.
Grassi2016.materials: Rate-dependent material model with specific strain limits for yield and failure; property assignment otherwise not stated.
Grassi2016.agreement_metric: Principal strains: R²=0.93, RMSE=10%, with 1,600 validated data points per specimen. Strength error: <2% in two specimens.
Grassi2016.result: Predicted femoral strength was accurate in two of three specimens; the third could not be reliably validated. Predicted failure location was very close to the experimental fracture rim.
Grassi2016.lessons: Full-field strain agreement was comparable to prior studies using 10–16 strain-gauge measurements. An accidental boundary-condition change compromised strength validation in one specimen; low sample size and a single loading condition limit conclusions.

Schileo2020.measurement: Experimental strain and strength measurements; failure load and location
Schileo2020.materials: CT-based FE models with CBM-derived cortical thickness and density; cortical-specific or independently optimised density–elasticity relationships; values not stated
Schileo2020.agreement_metric: Strain prediction errors: average, maximum, and 95th-percentile errors; failure load and location prediction
Schileo2020.result: CBM reduced average strain error by 30%; maximum and 95th-percentile errors were halved. At femoral neck locations, all error metrics were at least halved. Failure-load estimates worsened; failure-location estimates were equivalent to reference models.
Schileo2020.lessons: Subject-specific cortical thickness and density improved strain prediction, especially at the femoral neck. Changing the cortical density–elasticity relationship did not improve validation. The study recommends including local cortical estimates for physiological strain modelling.

Helgason2008.lessons: Methodological differences only partially explain inter-study variation. The authors recommend standardized bone testing and a benchmark study using a numerically validated model to predict experimental strains.

Henninger2010.lessons: Improper verification and validation can lead to false conclusions. The review recommends adopting V&V practices to improve credibility and peer acceptance of computational biomechanics models.

Anderson2007.lessons: The review recommends applying verification, validation, and sensitivity-study principles to computational biomechanics models to improve their analysis, interpretation, and peer acceptance.

Erdemir2012.lessons: Recommends reporting model identification and structure, simulation structure, verification, validation, and availability. More detailed reporting can clarify decisions and improve reproducibility, reusability, and sharing.

Nagaraja2024.loading: Compression-bending testing of spinal rod and pedicle screw constructs.
Nagaraja2024.materials: Medical-grade Ti-6Al-4V ELI; material property assignment not stated.
Nagaraja2024.agreement_metric: Stiffness and yield force comparisons; quantitative agreement not stated.
Nagaraja2024.lessons: The validated model was used to assess the cannulated screw design without additional testing; no error drivers or specific recommendations stated.

Garavelli2022.measurement: Digital Image Correlation (DIC) measured full-field vertebral surface displacements; quantitative CT used to generate the model
Garavelli2022.lessons: The pipeline predicted spine-segment displacement fields under physiological loading with good agreement, providing a first step toward credibility assessment. Error drivers and recommendations are not stated.

Maas2012.materials: Constitutive models are supported; specific assignments or values not stated.
Maas2012.solver: FEBio, a nonlinear implicit finite element framework
Maas2012.result: Verification problems were compared with analytical solutions or established FE codes; quantitative agreement not stated.
Maas2012.lessons: FEBio provides an open-source biomechanics-focused modeling environment. Verification is emphasized; no error drivers or specific recommendations are stated.

Rooks2022.n: not stated (four previously developed tibiofemoral models)
Rooks2022.loading: Varus-valgus simulations; one parameter changed at a time
Rooks2022.materials: Ligament and meniscus material models; continuum ligaments. Specific property assignments and values not stated.
Rooks2022.lessons: Sensitivity was model-dependent. Ligament prestretch, Young’s modulus, and attachment conditions strongly influenced outcomes; calibrating ligament properties is critical, and literature values may be unsuitable. Meniscus horn stiffness had small influence.

OpenFullJaw2022.loading: Finite element stability assessed under tipping and biting scenarios; load magnitudes and conditions not stated.
OpenFullJaw2022.agreement_metric: Hausdorff distance used to assess maximum deviations from input meshes; quantitative values and model-versus-experiment agreement not stated.
OpenFullJaw2022.result: Models were described as precise, with quality meshes suitable for various FE scenarios; no exact quantitative results stated.
OpenFullJaw2022.lessons: The pipeline reduces processing time and potential human-intervention bias. The 17-model dataset captures geometric variation and may support population studies of jaw biomechanics.

Henak2013.loading: Experimental physiological loading; load magnitude and protocol not stated.
Henak2013.measurement: Experimental contact stress and contact area measurements; cartilage compression characterization.
Henak2013.materials: Average neo-Hookean, average Veronda–Westmann, and specimen- and region-specific Veronda–Westmann hyperelastic cartilage models; coefficient values not stated.
Henak2013.agreement_metric: Average RMS error in contact stress.
Henak2013.result: Average RMS errors in contact stress were less than 25%; experimental measurements and FE predictions compared well across all three cartilage representations.
Henak2013.lessons: Average Veronda–Westmann coefficients accurately predicted peak and average contact stress, contact area, and patterns; specimen- and region-specific coefficients did not improve accuracy. Neo-Hookean models underpredicted peak stress in high-stress areas.

Liu2008AOB.loading: Tongue volume reduced by 15–17% in one animal per pair; no mechanical load stated.
Liu2008AOB.measurement: Longitudinal lateral and axial cephalograms, direct skull osteometry, and DEXA bone mineral density/content.
Liu2008AOB.result: No model-versus-experiment comparison or quantitative agreement metric reported.
Liu2008AOB.lessons: Tongue reduction slowed craniofacial skeletal growth and anterior dental arch expansion, especially at the mandibular symphysis and anterior arch; reduced functional loading may partly explain the effects.

Liu2008JOMS.loading: Natural mastication of pig chow; tongue loads on surrounding bones and facial surfaces were assessed.
Liu2008JOMS.measurement: Bone strain gauges, pressure transducers, and bilateral masseter EMG.
Liu2008JOMS.agreement_metric: not stated; no model comparison reported
Liu2008JOMS.result: Tongue volume was reduced by 23%–25%. In sham animals, principal bone surface strains were <100 με. Numerical model–experiment agreement: not stated.
Liu2008JOMS.lessons: Tongue loads were greater on mandibular lingual than maxillary/premaxillary palatal surfaces. Volume reduction decreased loads, especially in the anterior mouth. Tongue-generated masticatory loads were much smaller than those from masticatory muscles.

Deng2018.n: 11 sibling pairs (22 animals): 6 acute and 5 chronic pairs
Deng2018.loading: Electrical stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve trunk and branches, genioglossus, and styloglossus
Deng2018.measurement: Bone and suture strains measured with strain gauges; palatal and mandibular pressures measured with pressure transducers
Deng2018.result: not stated; no model-versus-experiment comparison reported
Deng2018.lessons: Tongue reduction lowered anterior and increased posterior loads during contractions. Anterior load reductions persisted, while posterior compensatory enhancement diminished with surgical healing.

Liu2026.measurement: Over 90 anatomical landmarks; 51 linear distances; tongue and masseter weights, sizes, and volumes
Liu2026.result: not stated; no model-versus-experiment comparison reported
Liu2026.lessons: Both tongue-base reduction and enlargement were associated with reduced craniofacial dimensions versus controls. Tongue-base volume correlated with mandibular ramus height in the reduction group (r = -0.804, p = 0.016).

Boosalis2026.loading: Simulated tongue pressure, lip-cheek pressure, and transseptal fiber-mediated interdental force, applied separately and together; load magnitudes not stated.
Boosalis2026.measurement: Simulated crown displacement; no experimental measurement stated.
Boosalis2026.lessons: Tongue pressure alone produced arch expansion and spacing; lip-cheek pressure and interdental force produced collapse, crowding, and mesial molar displacement. Combined loads produced incisor crowding, reduced intercanine width, and mesial molar displacement.

Alsaleem2025.loading: 1, 7, and 500 g/cm², representing rest, normal function, and tongue thrust; applied perpendicular to the lingual surface of the mandibular anterior region.
Alsaleem2025.solver: not stated; CAD software was used to develop the model.
Alsaleem2025.result: not stated; no model-versus-experiment agreement reported.
Alsaleem2025.lessons: Abnormal tongue thrust produced the highest von Mises stress (177 MPa) and displacement. Abnormal tongue forces may contribute to outward pressure and changes in the form and position of the mandibular anterior structure.

Sato1998.loading: Defined continuous or intermittent compressive pressure applied to the intermolar region of the hard palate; reported thresholds: 6.86 kPa continuous and ≥19.6 kPa intermittent.
Sato1998.measurement: Histopathological evaluation of osteoclastic bone resorption using a statistical criterion.
Sato1998.lessons: Bone resorption was pressure-threshold-regulated; the continuous-pressure threshold was lower than the intermittent-pressure threshold.

Jeannin2023.loading: Water-column-controlled pressure applied through a water-filled latex finger; calibration range 0–2.5 kPa, with possible extrapolation to 0–35 kPa after verifying sensor linearity.
Jeannin2023.measurement: Sensor output voltage versus applied pressure.
Jeannin2023.materials: Water-filled latex finger; material properties not stated.
Jeannin2023.result: Reliable linear pressure–voltage calibration reported over 0–2.5 kPa; no quantitative agreement values stated.
Jeannin2023.lessons: Account for latex-finger softening from the Mullins Effect and non-elastic deformation above a pressure threshold. Rigid-actuator position can strongly affect measurements; use one only to verify sensor linearity over a wider range.

Proffit1978.lessons: Resting tongue and lip pressures and periodontal forces are primary influences on tooth position; occlusion may affect vertical position through eruption. Respiratory needs alter posture and equilibrium. Deviate swallowing is likely adaptive; eruption disorders may be clinically underrecognized.

Reina2007.loading: Mastication loads, represented through stress levels in a bone-remodelling model.
Reina2007.materials: Predicted distributions of bone density and elastic constants; numerical values and assignment details not stated.
Reina2007.result: Density distribution and anisotropy were compared with clinical studies; agreement was described as reasonable, without quantitative metrics.
Reina2007.lessons: A phenomenological remodelling model previously applied to long bones was applied to the mandible, whose corpus behaves as a long bone. No specific error drivers or recommendations are stated.

Chou2015.loading: Clenching muscle forces from static linear optimization; other activities approximated by mandibular flexure and loading cycles.
Chou2015.measurement: CT images used to construct the model and observe bone-density distribution; no other experimental measurement stated.
Chou2015.materials: Material property assignment not stated; bone density regulated by a stress- and loading-cycle-dependent remodeling algorithm.
Chou2015.agreement_metric: not stated; no quantitative model-versus-experiment agreement reported.
Chou2015.result: Simulated density formed a tubular structure resembling CT observations. Edentulism could cause loss of up to one-third of mandibular bone mass.
Chou2015.lessons: Daily mechanical stimulation contributes to mandibular architecture; bone loss depends on the location and number of missing teeth.

Lin2010.loading: Axial and lateral loads; magnitudes not stated.
Lin2010.lessons: Implant position drove bone loss: ridge-axis placement increased it, especially buccally. Lateral loading slightly increased loss. Implant type did not significantly affect it. The study recommends aligning implants with occlusal force and reducing lateral occlusal force.

Kupczik2009.loading: Masticatory muscle forces estimated from cadaveric physiological cross-sectional areas; bite points sequentially applied at working-side teeth.
Kupczik2009.measurement: Validated against published experimental data; measurement type not stated.
Kupczik2009.lessons: SED was low in the supraorbital torus and consistently high in the zygomatic arch and infraorbital region. The torus may already be adapted to masticatory loads, or have a lower site-specific bone-deposition threshold.

Liang2024.lessons: Skull base contributes to anteroposterior facial growth; maxillary expansion contributes to dorsoventral facial growth and interacts with the orbits. Physical interactions among craniofacial components are important.

Profico2024.n: 51 head CT scans of normal individuals, selected from a database of 217
Profico2024.loading: Estimated masticatory muscle forces and bite forces; muscle forces increased across 0–48 months, and maximum bite force across 3–48 months.
Profico2024.measurement: CT imaging; no experimental strain or stress measurement stated.
Profico2024.lessons: Muscle and bite forces increase with age, and strain/stress patterns shift from the calvaria toward the face during development. The study raises questions about how mechanical-force changes may alter craniofacial morphology.

Lieberman2004.loading: Mastication of raw/dried versus cooked foods
Lieberman2004.measurement: In vivo masticatory strains and facial growth
Lieberman2004.result: not stated; no model-versus-experiment comparison reported
Lieberman2004.lessons: Raw food produced strains up to twice those from cooked food. Cooked-food hyraxes had approximately 10% less growth in ventral and posterior facial regions; results support reduced facial growth with food processing.

Formiga2026.loading: Simulated chewing stresses and superimposed vibration at 40 and 120 Hz.
Formiga2026.measurement: none (numerical simulations; CBCT changes are described as measurable, not measured)
Formiga2026.agreement_metric: not stated; no quantitative model-versus-experiment metric reported
Formiga2026.result: Chewing-only density approached 1.02–1.03 g/cm³. Vibration increased simulated steady-state density by about 3.5% at 40 Hz and 0.08–0.10 g/cm³ (about 10%) at 120 Hz.
Formiga2026.lessons: Vibration, especially at 120 Hz, broadened and homogenized anabolic adaptation. The model attributes the response to enhanced mechanotransductive efficiency; it recommends patient-specific vibration strategies.

Becker2024.materials: 12 heterogeneous material models using varied density–Young’s modulus relationships; derived from in vitro or computational methods and applied to cortical and trabecular bone.
Becker2024.lessons: Models vary substantially in estimated Young’s modulus and originate from other anatomical sites. Standardize experimental protocols, validate with combined simulations and experiments, and investigate mandibular anisotropy.

Daqiq2025.n: 66 records included; subject/specimen counts not stated (MBF studies n=60, muscle-force studies n=5, material-property studies n=5).
Daqiq2025.loading: Maximum bite force and muscle force were evaluated as mandibular FEA input parameters; specific applied loads not stated.
Daqiq2025.measurement: In vivo physical testing; specific measurement methods not stated.
Daqiq2025.materials: Mandible material properties were reviewed; assignments and values not stated.
Daqiq2025.lessons: MBF varies with sex, age, fracture status, postoperative follow-up, and denture type. The review provides input-parameter guidance and recommends further in vivo studies, especially to establish muscle forces and unknown parameters such as friction.

Walmsley2013.n: Seven species; specimen count not stated
Walmsley2013.materials: Compared heterogeneous and homogeneous material-property assignments; values not stated
Walmsley2013.lessons: Results were more sensitive to tooth position and linear load case than to material properties or scaling by volume or surface area. Interactions depended on assumptions and specimen shape. Select assumptions rigorously, incorporate biological context, validate where feasible, and otherwise perform sensitivity analyses.

Dechow2017.species: Rhesus macaques; compared with humans and baboons
Dechow2017.n: Six adult female mandibles; 30 cylindrical samples per mandible (180 samples total)
Dechow2017.measurement: Ultrasound velocity measurements and bone density measurements
Dechow2017.materials: Orthotropic cortical bone elastic properties computed from ultrasound velocities and density using Hooke's-law-based equations; values not stated
Dechow2017.lessons: Elastic properties varied by mandibular region, with similarities and differences versus humans and baboons; the biological and structural basis of these differences is poorly understood.

Peterson2006.measurement: Cortical thickness, density, elastic properties, and direction of greatest stiffness; measurement methods not stated
Peterson2006.lessons: Material properties and principal stiffness-axis orientations vary regionally; maxillary elastic properties are more variable than mandibular ones. Incorporating these properties into finite-element models should improve accuracy and reliability.

Hillam2015.loading: Physiological and unusual activities, including vigorous activity, heading a heavy medicine/exercise ball, biting, and facial contortions; ground reaction exceeded 5 times body weight during vigorous activity.
Hillam2015.measurement: In vivo bone strain measured at the tibia and cranium; measurement instrument not stated.
Hillam2015.result: Tibial strain exceeded 0.2%; maximum parietal strain was 0.0192%. Peak tibial strain rate exceeded parietal strain rate by more than 5-fold.
Hillam2015.lessons: Skull and tibia experience markedly different strain environments and may have different regulatory influences. Biting strains were not dependent on bite force and could arise from facial contortions without tooth contact.

Fox2020.loading: Bone- or dental-borne rapid palatal expanders activated at one turn per minute for 30 turns.
Fox2020.measurement: DVRT measured midpalatal suture separation; single-element strain gauges measured strain at the alveolar bone, zygomaticomaxillary sutures, and internasal sutures.
Fox2020.lessons: Bone-borne expansion achieved more successful midpalatal suture expansion (69% vs 27%), with greater and earlier separation. Dental-borne expansion produced higher alveolar-bone strain; bone-borne expansion tended toward higher zygomaticomaxillary strain.

Oliveira2020.loading: MARPE or Hyrax activated 25 times for rapid maxillary expansion.
Oliveira2020.measurement: Strain gauges at MPS, MPM, MZ, and MPP; intermolar distance and suture width measured before activation and at activations 20 and 25.
Oliveira2020.result: No computational model or model–experiment agreement reported; one MARPE device produced 1.7 mm posterior opening.
Oliveira2020.lessons: MARPE developed more constant tensions during activation at the MPS and MZ; Hyrax tension was lower during activations 16–25. Accumulated MPS tension exceeded that at the other sutures.

Ichim2007.loading: Masticatory load during chewing; details not stated
Ichim2007.lessons: Strain patterns differ between alveolar and mid-corpus regions; mid-corpus strains alternate between buccal and lingual aspects on working and balancing sides. Cortical asymmetry was not related to mastication-generated strain patterns.

Fung2017.n: 33 metatarsals from seven cadaveric feet; training set n=17, test set n=16.
Fung2017.measurement: Strain gauges; CT imaging for subject-specific FE models.
Fung2017.materials: CT-based density-modulus assignment using a published relationship and optimized relationships; separate trabecular and cortical equations were also tested.
Fung2017.agreement_metric: Experimental-versus-predicted strain correlation: training r²≥0.95; test r²≥0.94. Optimized equations reduced maximum error by 10%–20% versus the published equation.
Fung2017.result: Optimized equations produced an X=Y-type relationship between experimental and FE-predicted strains.
Fung2017.lessons: Optimized material-property assignment improved maximum error; separate trabecular and cortical equations did not improve predictions. Models were considered accurate enough to investigate interventions to reduce metatarsal strain.

Bright2012.n: Not stated; models validated against data from the same specimen.
Bright2012.materials: Material property assignment not stated; local bone material-property variations were not accounted for.
Bright2012.agreement_metric: Quantitative metric and values not stated; qualitative model fit to experimental strain data.
Bright2012.result: Adding sutures changed predicted strain patterns but reduced model accuracy compared with the model without sutures.
Bright2012.lessons: Sutures alone did not explain model inaccuracies. Unmodeled variation in local bone material properties was suggested as a possible cause.

MehariAbraha2019.measurement: In vivo bone strain data used for validation; measurement method not stated
MehariAbraha2019.materials: PDL Young’s modulus varied across 0.07–1750 MPa; other material assignments not stated
MehariAbraha2019.lessons: PDL presence changed local and global surface strains; effects away from alveoli were limited (~200–300 με). Modulus variation had little effect on global strains. PDL may be omitted for cross-species strain-gradient comparisons; sensitivity analysis is recommended when absolute strain values matter.

Marinescu2005.loading: Simplified loading regime; force orientation varied; magnitude not stated
Marinescu2005.materials: Isotropic and heterogeneous orthotropic models; property values not stated
Marinescu2005.agreement_metric: Quantitative metric and exact values not stated
Marinescu2005.result: Heterogeneous orthotropic and edentulous models were more congruent with experimental strains; isotropic and dentate models agreed less well.
Marinescu2005.lessons: Small load-direction errors substantially changed predicted strains. Failure to model the periodontal ligament may explain the edentulous model’s better fit; teeth may not add much stiffness without occlusal loads.

Fitton2012.loading: Finite element simulations of second-molar biting with controlled bite-force magnitude; varied bite location and masticatory muscle activation patterns, including muscle-group inclusion/exclusion.
Fitton2012.agreement_metric: not stated; no quantitative model-versus-experiment comparison reported
Fitton2012.result: No quantitative agreement values reported. Bite location affected cranial deformation more than muscle-activation variation; superficial masseter activation most influenced zygomatic deformation.
Fitton2012.lessons: Reasonable muscle-load approximations generally yield acceptable deformation estimates, except zygomatic deformation is sensitive to superficial masseter activation. Judge muscle-force error against the effect under investigation.

Cuff2015.measurement: Ex-vivo strains from cranial bone and rhamphotheca; measurement method not stated
Cuff2015.materials: Segmented cortical and trabecular bone, sutures, and keratinous rhamphotheca; isotropic properties from literature or nanoindentation
Cuff2015.agreement_metric: Strain orientations were within 10° in some regions; correlation was generally weak elsewhere
Cuff2015.result: Models generally matched peak-strain locations and rostral deformation mode, but were too stiff in high-strain regions and too elastic in low-strain regions. Rhamphotheca principal strains were overpredicted.
Cuff2015.lessons: Sutures affect strain magnitudes and patterns across the skull; model sutures and rhamphotheca. Peak locations and some deformation patterns were reproduced, but matching experimental strains remains problematic.

Rayfield2011.loading: Hydraulic force applied at the beak tip, similar to forces measured during pecking experiments; exact force not stated.
Rayfield2011.measurement: Strain gauges at four sites (dorsal and ventral dentary, medial and lateral surangular); CT scans used to create FE models.
Rayfield2011.materials: Isotropic, homogeneous material properties; values not stated. Models had solid internal geometry.
Rayfield2011.agreement_metric: Compared strain magnitudes, orientations, patterns, and maximum-to-minimum principal strain ratios; no quantitative agreement statistics stated.
Rayfield2011.result: Dentary predictions closely matched experiments across reported strain measures. Postdentary strain magnitudes were predicted, but orientations and ratios were inaccurate; exact numbers not stated.
Rayfield2011.lessons: Postdentary mismatch may reflect intramandibular sutures or more cancellous bone. Findings emphasize geometry and sutures and support simple FE models while noting validation priorities may differ among taxa.

Casas2007.loading: Regulation baseball (142 g) impacting the medial maxilla at 14 m/s
Casas2007.measurement: Three-axis strain-gauge rosettes at the medial palate and both canine fossae; experimental displacements and principal strains
Casas2007.agreement_metric: Difference between experimental and calculated principal strains
Casas2007.lessons: The model was considered geometrically accurate at approximately 74,000 degrees of freedom. No specific source of error or recommendation was stated.

Fang2007.loading: 4 mm transverse displacement applied to the bone anchor
Fang2007.measurement: none; CBCT Hounsfield units were used to assign material properties
Fang2007.materials: Heterogeneous properties assigned based on CBCT Hounsfield unit values; specific values not stated. 3 mm diameter cylindrical bone anchor.
Fang2007.lessons: Displacement and stress–strain trends were appropriate, and stress patterns resembled literature. No significant difference was found between anchor inclination angles. The model may support understanding and patient-specific treatment development.

RiveraTapia2025.n: not stated (79 studies identified; 13 reported FEM parameters and 6 included clinical validation)
RiveraTapia2025.materials: Many models used idealised isotropic, linear-elastic properties; values not stated
RiveraTapia2025.lessons: FEM maps stress and strain, but clinical prediction is limited by simplified anatomy, variable meshes and loading, and inadequate validation. Authors recommend detailed patient-specific anatomy, physiological boundary conditions, and validation against longitudinal CBCT data.

Sun2011.loading: Acute palatal expansion using hyrax expanders
Sun2011.measurement: Strain gauges at buccal alveolar bone and circummaxillary sutures; intermolar width measured from dental casts
Sun2011.lessons: Expansion caused occlusal-apical compression at anchor-tooth buccal alveolar bone and generally physiologic-level circummaxillary suture strains; suture strain was compressive at maxillary-zygomatic and zygomatic-temporal sutures, tensile at maxillary-premaxillary.

Szwedowski2010.loading: Less than 150 N tensile force applied through the masseter muscle to the zygomatic arch origin at 4 orientations.
Szwedowski2010.measurement: In vitro strain measurements at 12 locations across 16 independent channels; 3 trials of 500 recorded data points per orientation.
Szwedowski2010.materials: Shell elements modeled thin cortical bone; material properties not stated.
Szwedowski2010.result: r = 0.57 overall; r = 0.70 after excluding comparisons in regions requiring greater modeling assumptions.
Szwedowski2010.lessons: Regions requiring greater modeling assumptions reduced agreement. Future validation should place strain gauges using FE-predicted strain patterns as a guide.

Erdemir2019.lessons: Modeling decisions can be subjective and affect conclusions and reproducibility. The project aims to document workflows, deviations, models, results, and comparisons transparently to identify factors underlying poor reproducibility.

Erdemir2021.result: No quantitative model-versus-experiment agreement reported. Uncalibrated models showed a large spread in kinematic outputs.
Erdemir2021.lessons: Differences in anatomical landmark choices drove variation in kinematics despite consistent boundary conditions and coordinate-system convention. All teams deviated from initial plans, showing model development is flexible and difficult to plan.

Erdemir2022.n: not stated (nine studies assessed; specimen/subject count not given)
Erdemir2022.lessons: Reporting and perceived reproducibility were relatively low, highlighting opportunities to improve reporting practices. Reported category proportions ranged 0.31–0.77; reproducibility proportions ranged 0.22–0.44.

Marghoub2019.loading: not stated; model simulated calvarial growth
Marghoub2019.measurement: MicroCT imaging and morphological measurements at P3, P10, and P20
Marghoub2019.result: not stated; no quantitative model-versus-experiment agreement values reported
Marghoub2019.lessons: Models were sensitive to input-parameter choices but predicted overall skull growth and captured WT–mutant differences.

Kieser2008.loading: Swallowed 10 ml of water while seated upright.
Kieser2008.measurement: Eight miniature absolute-pressure transducers mounted on a custom chrome-cobalt palatal appliance; simultaneous intraoral pressure recordings.
Kieser2008.materials: Chrome-cobalt appliance; material properties not stated.
Kieser2008.agreement_metric: Not stated; no model comparison reported.
Kieser2008.lessons: Intraoral pressures included significant negative values during swallowing and varied markedly between individuals. The appliance enabled simultaneous measurements at eight locations during function.

Lima2025.n: 24 studies (18 primary studies and 6 reviews); participant count not stated
Lima2025.result: No quantitative model-versus-experiment agreement reported. OMT effectiveness could not be conclusively confirmed; level 2 evidence suggests possible benefit for OMDs following orthognathic surgery.
Lima2025.lessons: Evidence was limited, with no level 1 evidence and only four RCTs. Further well-designed RCTs are needed.

Xiao2026.measurement: Dental impressions and digital measurements of maxillary arch dimensions and palatal depth; questionnaires and clinical examination of oral habits and muscle function
Xiao2026.result: not stated; no model-versus-experiment comparison reported
Xiao2026.lessons: Early myofunctional training may benefit maxillary arch development and orofacial muscle function; findings are preliminary and may support preventive orthodontic strategies.

Rafferty2019.species: Normal-snouted pigs, minipigs, and Yucatan minipigs
Rafferty2019.n: Varying sample sizes; exact counts not stated
Rafferty2019.loading: Mastication and cyclic tensile loading of the nasofrontal suture
Rafferty2019.measurement: Computed tomography, histology, and strain-gauge recordings
Rafferty2019.lessons: Yucatan sutures were narrower and showed hyperossification-related features, but were not fused and responded similarly to cyclic tensile loading. Before fusion, sutures may be amenable to treatment promoting growth.

Prado2016.species: Humans, human fossil relatives, chimpanzees, Sapajus apella, and other nonhuman primates
Prado2016.measurement: Review of published in vivo bone-strain and finite-element studies; specific measurement methods not stated
Prado2016.materials: Specific material-property assignments not stated; available data do not support facial pillars and buttresses in humans or Sapajus apella
Prado2016.result: No quantitative model-versus-experiment agreement values reported in the abstract
Prado2016.lessons: Zygomatic-complex deformation emphasizes bending and shear, not pillar-like loading. A zygomatic pillar lacks support; replace the pillar-and-buttress model with FEMs that better represent in vivo function and inform implant and fracture-repair research.

Kok2021.measurement: Bilateral digital image correlation measured full-field strains on medial and lateral femoral neck; experimental peak forces were measured.
Kok2021.materials: Strain-rate-dependent material description with separate yield and fracture strain limits in tension and compression; values not stated.
Kok2021.agreement_metric: R² for predicted versus measured fracture force and strains; distance from predicted fracture initiation to experimental fracture line.
Kok2021.result: Fracture force R²=0.92; strain R²=0.87 medial and 0.74 lateral. Fracture initiation was within 3 mm of the experimental line for 8/12 subjects.
Kok2021.lessons: Lower lateral strain correlation was attributed to irregular cortex and vessel holes. Bilateral strain and peak-force validation supports more extensive validation of femoral FE models for sideways falls.

Dahan2016.loading: Loaded at three inclination angles; head displacement was then applied to induce fracture.
Dahan2016.measurement: CT scans and strain-gauge measurements; experimental strains compared with FE-predicted strains.
Dahan2016.materials: Inhomogeneous isotropic properties assigned using the femur E(ρash) relationship; values not stated.
Dahan2016.solver: High-order p-FE and classical h-FE; software not stated.
Dahan2016.agreement_metric: Linear regression slope m=1.09; R²=0.98 for predicted versus measured elastic-range strains.
Dahan2016.result: Excellent elastic-range strain agreement; p-FE and h-FE results were similar.
Dahan2016.lessons: The femur E(ρash) relationship worked for humeri. Contact FEA did not reproduce experimental boundary conditions; a nonlinear model is needed for post-cortical-fracture behavior, with further experiments under FEA-representable conditions.

Jung2010.loading: Open mouth, gently closed lips, closed compartments after generating negative pressure, and swallowing
Jung2010.measurement: Simultaneous atmospheric-pressure monitoring with a digital manometer in the vestibular inter-occlusal space (IOS) and sub-palatal space (SPS)
Jung2010.agreement_metric: not stated; no quantitative model-versus-experiment agreement reported
Jung2010.result: not stated for model-versus-experiment agreement; mean pressures (IOS, SPS) were 0.0, −0.08 mbar (OC); −0.16, −1.0 (SC); −48.79, −81.86 (CCN); and −29.25, −62.51 (SW)
Jung2010.lessons: Both null hypotheses were rejected. Findings indicate two distinct intra-oral functional compartments and help explain negative intra-oral pressures at rest.

Proffit1975.lessons: The abstract suggests resting lip pressure, rather than tongue pressure during swallowing, may be the relevant environmental factor in dental arch dimensions; tongue size and strength are not unusually large.

Herring2005ontogeny.n: 45 dry skulls; number of strain-tested piglets not stated
Herring2005ontogeny.loading: Functional mastication and masseter muscle stimulation
Herring2005ontogeny.measurement: Bone strain and skull dimensions; measurement technique not stated
Herring2005ontogeny.lessons: Piglet strain patterns were more variable than in older pigs. Growth-related arch shape changes may make strain more predictable; unfamiliarity with hard food, other muscles, and tooth proximity may also contribute. Skeletons are not pre-adapted for specific functional loads.
